newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy industry demands change to government policy.
newsitem.headline: Italy industry demands change to government policy.

text.p: Italian industrialists, enraged by government economic policy, told Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Thursday he would have to change direction if he wanted to join the single European currency from the start.

Giorgio Fossa, chairman of Italian business confederation Confindustria, told an extraordinary meeting of the organisation that the centre-left government was suffocating business in its bid to overhaul the economy.
"Today we are underlining our opposition to an economic policy that we feel is wrong for the country," Fossa said in a hard-hitting speech to some 2,000 delegates from across Italy.

Hundreds more business leaders watched the assembly in a live video link relayed around the country. Prodi's government faces confidence motions in both houses of parliament over the next three days, as a result of the Communist Refoundation party's refusal to back deployment of Italian troops in a security force for Albania.

Fossa called on Prodi to withdraw a recently presented mini-budget, which is designed to cut 15.5 trillion lire ($9.3 billion) off the 1997 deficit, and said lawyers were investigating whether the package was legally valid.

The budget, needed to lower Italy's public administration deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), includes measures to raise six trillion lire by forcing firms to pay tax advances on their huge pool of severance payment funds.

Confidustria had urged Prodi to seek savings by slashing back at welfare costs, but plans for cuts to social spending were vetoed by the hard left Communist Refondation, which secures the government's parliamentary majority.

"This mini-budget is the last straw," Fossa said. "A government which accepts the demands of one political or social group and doesn't do what it knows necessary, is a government incapable of heading the transition towards Europe," he added.
Marco Tronchetti Provera, head of tyre and cable company Pirelli, said Italian business was suffering under Prodi's administration.
"This is a government which is mocking us and parliament is not giving us the means to be competitive. This...has to end," Tronchetti Provera told the assembly to loud applause.

However Prodi, in an address to the Senate (upper house) on Thursday, called on industrialists to stop complaining, saying a fall in interest rates over the past year had compensated for the higher tax burden caused by the mini-budget.

"I would really appreciate it if the business world recognised that the fall in the cost of borrowing had brought proportionally larger benefits than any temporary increase in the fiscal burden," Prodi said.
Interest rates have fallen steadily over the past year, pushed lower by a sharp drop in inflation.
Prodi added that he could not "understand or accept the position adopted by industrial associations."
However both Prodi and the industrialists agreed that a review of the welfare state could not be delayed further.
"It is no longer possible to put off the reform of public spending and an overly heavy welfare state," Fossa said. "It cannot be put off a day longer," Prodi told parliament. $1 = 1,670 lire
